Intel Sinks 8% as Midterm Chip Sell-Off Deepens ©@Vedat OGUZCAN from Getty Images via Canva, @Daniel CHETRONI from Daniel Chetroni via Canva
Key Takeaways

Intel fell 8% today as chip stocks sold off on worries that Democrats' midterm wins could slow the data-center buildout.

Intel's problem is supply: it can't make enough server chips, so a slower buildout hurts it less than most.

Microchip Technology fell harder than Intel, a sign the selling hit chipmakers across the board.

With estimates already cut and the forward P/E below its five-year average, much of the bad news looks priced in.

Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) fell 8% today as chip stocks sold off for a second straight day, on worries that Democrats' bigger-than-expected midterm wins will slow the data-center buildout.

That's less than the semiconductor index's 11% drop. And Microchip Technology (MCHP:NASDAQ), which also makes chips in its own fabs, fell 13% with no news of its own.

What exactly happened

Democrats won both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's midterms, and on Wednesday, Democratic Rep. Yassamin Ansari called for a pause on advanced AI development until regulations are in place.

Intel came in bruised: the stock is down nearly half in a month after guiding fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion on Oct. 29.

Intel's problem is supply

What held that guide back was supply. A two-week shutdown at its Kiryat Gat fab in Israel cost it roughly $300 million of revenue, and a substrate shortage is limiting how many Xeon server chips it can ship. CEO Lip-Bu Tan called unlocking Xeon supply Intel's "immediate priority."

So a slower buildout hurts Intel less, since it already has more server demand than it can fill. If Congress slows data-center spending, though, that demand could cool before supply catches up.

The selling also hit chipmakers without Intel's troubles. Microchip's June-quarter net sales rose 38% to $1.49 billion, and it guided the September quarter up 7% to 9% from there. If its next report shows that recovery holding, today's drop had little to do with its business.

At today's price, it's around 40x. That's still far above the 10x to 18x it traded at from 2014 to 2022, so the stock is priced for a turnaround.

title: Is AMD Stock a Buy as AI Revenue Soars?

Is AMD Stock a Buy as AI Revenue Soars?
Geoffrey Seiler, The Motley Fool

AMD
NVDA
INTC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) turned in strong third-quarter results, as its data center revenue nearly doubled. The semiconductor stock has had a strong year, up over 125% going into the report, but has more recently been caught in the AI infrastructure sell-off, and it also took a hit because of rival Intel's (NASDAQ: INTC) weak guidance.

Let's take a closer look at the company's earnings results and prospects to see why I think the stock is a buy.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Strong AI growth ahead

While AMD and Intel are both competitors in the central processing unit (CPU) space, the two companies are quite different. AMD has been taking share from Intel in the server CPU market for years, and has also begun making inroads with its graphics processing units (GPUs). As such, AMD is much more about serving data center clients, while Intel is much more heavily exposed to the weakening PC market, which has come under pressure from rising memory costs.

AMD is seeing pressure in this area as well, projecting a double-digit percentage decline in unit shipments in the PC market next year. Overall, its client and gaming segment revenue fell 8% to $3.7 billion. Client revenue, where its PC business sits, rose 7% to $2.9 billion, while gaming revenue fell 40% to $773 million.

AMD's biggest unit and growth driver, however, is its data center segment. This accounted for 64% of its Q3 revenue, and the company projected it will represent more than 80% of its revenue in 2027.

AMD's data center revenue surged 97% in Q3 to $8.5 billion, powered by strong demand for its Epyc CPUs and MI450 GPUs. The company began shipping its new Venice CPUs in the quarter, which it expects will help it gain even more market share. It continues to see the server CPU market growing to a $220 billion total addressable market by 2030, as demand surges due to the rise of AI agents.

At the same time, the company said AI labs, hyperscalers, and cloud computing providers all increased GPU deployments, helping drive record revenue. It said it delivered its Helios full-rack AI system, which combines its GPUs, CPUs, and networking components, this quarter to lead customers, including Anthropic, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle. It said it expects Helios revenue to ramp up in Q4 as OEM (original equipment manufacturer) and ODM (original design manufacturer) partners begin to ship the systems.

Key Takeaways

ASML shares fell 8% today in a post-election chip sell-off, and Everpure fell even harder.

ASML had no news, and its customers' down payments show demand for its machines still outruns supply.

Analysts expect ASML's normalized EPS to roughly triple from 2025 to 2028, yet its forward P/E sits well below its five-year average.

ASML gives its first 2027 outlook with fourth-quarter results on Jan. 27.

ASML Holding (ASML:NASDAQ) fell 8% today as the post-election chip sell-off ran into a second day. Storage maker Everpure (P:NYSE) slid 16%.

A second scare in a week

Chip stocks fell on fears that Democrats' larger-than-expected midterm wins will slow data-center spending. Qualcomm's light guidance after Wednesday's close made it worse. For ASML, it's the second drop in a week, after it fell 6% in Intel's chip rout.

Stocks closer to the data centers fell harder. Applied Digital (APLD:NASDAQ), which builds them, fell 16% after election results in Texas raised worries about data-center permits. Ciena (CIEN:NYSE), whose optical gear links them, lost 15% as optics peer Coherent slid after its own report.

ASML sits two steps further back than Applied Digital and Ciena: it sells machines to the chipmakers that supply data centers.

Demand still outruns supply

Nobody else sells EUV machines, and ASML can't build them fast enough. Management says its planned supply for 2027 and 2028 won't fully meet demand, and customers want to order for 2029 and 2030.

They're paying ahead, too: noncurrent contract liabilities, which hold customers' down payments, jumped from €3.6 billion to €9.3 billion in the third quarter of 2026.

Analysts see ASML's normalized EPS roughly tripling, from €24.7 in 2025 to €76.2 in 2028:

ASML Holding (ASML): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, € per share, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

Nothing in today's sell-off came from ASML, so I don't see a reason for analysts to cut those numbers.

A much cheaper stock

The stock is another matter. It traded at 47x forward earnings at the end of June, and 25x before today's drop, well below its five-year average of 34x:

Today's drop takes it to about 23x.

The way I see it, the market just marked down a business whose customers are lining up to pay in advance, and that looks like an opportunity.

The market's fear is real enough: ASML's plans assume chipmakers keep spending through at least 2028, and if data-center building slows, their orders would too. Plus, ASML's CFO has said the MATCH Act, a proposed US ban on DUV immersion sales to China, could come up after the midterms. China is about 20% of ASML's expected 2026 sales.

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) witnessed a brutal sell-off last week after releasing its third-quarter results on Oct. 29, primarily due to weaker-than-expected guidance that led investors to press the panic button.

Intel's personal computer (PC)-focused client business is not in the best shape now due to a steep drop in PC sales. Of course, Intel needed to live up to Wall Street's expectations to justify the impressive surge the stock has witnessed since the beginning of 2025. However, the weakness in the PC market is beyond Intel's control.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Moreover, Intel is doing well in data centers, with its artificial intelligence (AI)-focused server chips in solid demand from hyperscalers and AI companies. Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) is one such company that will deploy Intel's server central processing units (CPUs) in large numbers. Let's look at the reasons why the Oracle contract could be a big one for Intel.

Image source: Getty Images.

Intel is poised to win big from Oracle's AI data center build-out

Just a couple of days ahead of Intel's quarterly report, the semiconductor giant announced a multiyear collaboration with Oracle to deploy its Xeon server CPUs. Oracle will deploy Intel's current and future generations of Xeon server CPUs to handle agentic AI workloads on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI).

This bodes well for Intel, given that OCI revenue has been growing at a brisk pace. Oracle reported a 121% year-over-year increase in OCI revenue in the previous quarter to $7.4 billion. This segment can sustain its terrific momentum over the long run owing to Oracle's $664 billion in remaining performance obligation (RPO), the total value of contracts the company has yet to fulfill.

Oracle expects to accelerate the conversion of its RPO into revenue going forward, driven by the company's significant investments to bring additional data center capacity online. Intel will provide Oracle with "additional capacity and planned processor capabilities as customers extend existing enterprise systems with AI."

This should ensure strong growth in Intel's server CPU business. Notably, Intel estimates that the total addressable market (TAM) for server CPUs could increase 5x over the next five years, reaching $400 billion. Chipzilla's ability to land a major customer like Oracle should allow it to capture a significant share of this massive opportunity.

Intel (INTC) CEO Lip-Bu Tan bought $10 million of stock two days after its worst crash since 1974, and it's already down 10%.

Tan's two 2026 purchases show a 25% paper loss, yet his total Intel investment, including his 2025 buy at $24, is up $31 million.

Zinsner says 2027 likely won't bring positive cash flow, and Intel's weak guidance makes Tan's $10 million vote of confidence matter little.

Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) CEO Lip-Bu Tan added to his position two sessions after the stock's worst day since 1974. By the close on November 4, 2026, that purchase was already showing a loss. A Form 4 signed November 4 shows that his family trust bought 150,000 shares of Intel on Monday, November 2. He paid a weighted average of $64.7312 a share, for a total of $9,709,680.

Intel

Intel closed November 4 at $58.27, down 3.77%. Tan's two purchases this year cost about $20 million combined, and they now show a paper loss of about $4.8 million. So you have a CEO putting his own money in at lower prices while the company's guidance points to a year of spending more cash than it brings in.

INTC Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
What the November Form 4 Shows

The filing uses transaction code P, which marks an open-market purchase. The Rule 10b5-1 box is unchecked, so the trade was not set up in advance under a trading plan. The form lists a price range of $64.705 to $64.735 but gives no trade times.

Intel opened at $65.40 that day, so Tan probably bought early in the session, although the filing does not say so. The stock then fell 8.80% and closed at $59.97, about 7.4% below what he paid.

After the purchase, the trust held 1,464,669 shares. Tan also holds 16,471 shares directly and 500 in a 401(k). The filing gives no reason for the purchase.
